# Introduction

An implicit assumption made when fitting a regression model is that **all observations should be equally reliable and have approximately equal role** in determining the regression results and in influencing conclusions.

- A [**leverage point**]{style="color:blue"} is an observation that is unusual in the predictor space.
- An [**outlier**]{style="color:blue"} is an observation whose response does not match the pattern of the fitted model.
- An [**influential observation**]{style="color:blue"} is one that causes a substantial change in the fitted model based on its inclusion or deletion from the model.
- An influential observation is usually either a leverage point, an outlier, or a combination of the two.  


![Influential Observations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aspiegler/Applied-Regression/main/Images/17-outlier-leverage.png)


Influential observations result from a number of sources. For example:

- They may be due to errors in measurement or due to errors in data entry.
  - We can check the data for coding errors.
- We may randomly select an unusual or unlikely observation during data collection. 
  - We should not remove these observations without further investigation.

# Leverage Points

The [**leverage (or hat) values**]{style="color:blue"} are the diagonal elements of the hat matrix $H=X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T$.  The $i^{\text{th}}$ diagonal position of the hat matrix, $h_{ii}$, is the $i^{\text{th}}$ leverage (or hat) value. 


## Computing the Hat Matrix and Leverage Values

```{r}
data(savings, package = "faraway") # load data
lmod <- lm(sr ~ ., data = savings) #fit full model
faraway::sumary(lmod)  # truncated summary output
```

Here we construct the hat matrix $H=X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T$

```{r}
X <- model.matrix(lmod)
hat_mat <- X %*% solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X)
round(head(hat_mat[1:6,1:6]), 4)  # first 6 rows/cols
```

There is a built-in `base` R function `hatvalues()` which does this as well.

```{r}
h <- hatvalues(lmod)
h[1:6]
```

## Interpreting Leverage Values

The predicted response $\hat{y}_i$ for observation $i$ can be written as a linear combination of the observed responses, $y_i$, using the hat matrix, $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = H \mathbf{y}$:

$$\hat{y}_i = h_{i1} y_1 +  h_{i2} y_2 + \ldots + {\color{blue}{h_{ii} y_i}} + \ldots + h_{in} y_n.$$

The $i^{\text{th}}$ leverage value, $h_{ii}$, measures the influence observed response $y_i$ has on the predicted value $\hat{y}_i$. Using derivatives, we have:

$$h_{ii} = \frac{\partial \hat{y}_i}{\partial y_i}.$$

- If $h_{ii}$ is small (close to 0), then the observed response plays a small role. 
- If $h_{ii}$ is small (close to 1), then the observed response plays a large role. 
- We have $\sum h_{ii} = p$, the number of regression coefficients (including intercept).


```{r}
# using hat values as weights
t(hat_mat[1, ]) %*% savings$sr  # 1st row of H dot obs response
fitted(lmod)[1]  # predicted value of observation 1
```

```{r}
# sum of hat values is p
sum(h)
```


:::{.callout-tip}
See the [Appendix](#sec-append) for proofs of properties that $0 \leq h_{ii} \leq 1$ and $\sum h_{ii} = p$.
:::

## Identifying Influential Points

Common criteria for identifying influential points using leverage values are any values exceeding $\frac{3p}{n}$ or $\frac{2p}{n}$ should be scrutinized as an influential observation where $p$ is the number of regression coefficients (including the intercept) and $n$ is the number of observations.

## Half-Normal Plots

A [**half-normal plot**]{style="color:blue"} of the leverage values can be used to identify observations with unusually high leverage. A half-normal plot is a modified Q-Q plot that compares the sorted hat values against the quantiles of a [half-normal distribution](https://distribution-explorer.github.io/continuous/halfnormal.html).


The steps are to producing a half-normal plot for $x_1, \ldots , x_n$ are:

1. Sort the data:  $h_{\lbrack 1 \rbrack} \leq h_{\lbrack 2 \rbrack} \leq \ldots \leq h_{\lbrack n \rbrack}$.

```{r}
h_sort <- sort(h)  # sort hatvalues
```

2. Compute $u_i = F^{-1} \left(\frac{n+i}{2n+1} \right)$, where $F$ denotes the CDF of $N(0,1)$.

```{r}
# compute half-normal quantiles
u <- numeric(50)

for (i in 1:50) {
  u[i] <- qnorm( (50 + i) / (2*50 + 1) )
}

head(round(u, 4))  # u_1, u_2, ... , u_6
tail(round(u, 4))  # u_45, u_46, ... u_50
```


3. Plot $h_{\lbrack i \rbrack}$  versus $u_i$.


```{r}
plot(h_sort ~ u)  # half-normal plot
```



The leverage points are the points in the plot that diverge substantially from the rest of the data.

- If the half-normal plot is approximately a straight line of points, then there are no leverage points.
- **If the half-normal plot is curved (looks like a hockey stick), then the points on the curvy part (the bendy part of the stick) are leverage points.**


The `halfnorm()` function from the `faraway` package generates a half-normal plot.


```{r}
# library(faraway)
countries <- row.names(savings)  # label with country name 
halfnorm(h, nlab = 2, labs = countries, ylab = "leverage")
```

### Example With No Leverage Points


```{r}
#| echo: false
data(state)
statedata <- data.frame(state.x77, row.names = state.abb)
names.state <- row.names(statedata)
lmod2 <- lm(Employed ~ ., data = longley)
h2 <- hatvalues(lmod2)
halfnorm(h2, nlab = 2, labs = names.state, ylab = "leverage")
```

## Index Plots

An [**index plot**]{style="color:blue"} of the leverage values can also be used to identify leverage points.  

- An index plot plots the statistic of an observation versus its observation number.
- You want to focus on observations where the statistics are large or small relative to the other values.

The `infIndexPlot()` function from the `car` package generates index plots related to many influence-related statistics (such as leverage value).


```{r}
#| warning: false
#library(car)
infIndexPlot(lmod, vars = "hat")
```


# Identifying outliers

An [**outlier**]{style="color:blue"} is a point that does not fit the current model.

- An outlier is context specific!  An outlier for one model may not be an outlier for a different model.


## Leave-One-Out Statistics

[**Leave-one-out statistics**]{style="color:blue"} are statistics computed from the model fitted without the $i^{\text{th}}$ observation. We use the subscript $(i)$ means that these statistics were estimated for the model fitted without the $i^{\text{th}}$ observation.


- $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(i)}$ is the vector of leave-one-out estimated coefficients.
- $\widehat{y}_{(i)}$ is the leave-one-out fitted value for the $i^{\text{th}}$ observation.
- $\widehat{\epsilon}_{(i)} = y_{i} - \widehat{y}_{(i)}$ is the leave-one-out residual for the $i^{\text{th}}$ observation.
- $\widehat{\sigma}_{(i)}$ is the leave-one-out estimate of the standard deviation of the leave-one-out error.  
  - $\displaystyle \widehat{\sigma}_{(i)} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{RSS}_{(i)} }{n-p-1}}$


```{r}
# Zambia is observation 46
loo_data <- savings[-46,]
loo_mod <- lm(sr ~ ., data = loo_data)
faraway::sumary(loo_mod)
```

If the [**leave-one-out residual**]{style="color:blue"} (deleted residual) $\widehat{\epsilon}_{(i)}$ is "large", then observation $i$ is an outlier.

```{r}
zambia_df <- as.data.frame(savings[46,])
(res_zambia <- savings[46,1] - predict(loo_mod, new = zambia_df))
```


::: {.callout-note}
The OLS residuals may not be suitable for identifying outliers since truly influential observations will pull the fitted model close to themselves, making the residual smaller.
:::

When deciding how "large" does a leave-one-out residual, $\widehat{\epsilon}_{(i)}$, need to be for the observation to be an outlier, the answer as usual is *it depends* on how large the residuals of leave-one-out model are overall.


```{r}
# loo residuals for other observations
head(sort(round(residuals(loo_mod),4)), 3)  # most negative residuals
tail(sort(round(residuals(loo_mod),4)), 3)  # most positive residuals
```

## Studentized Residuals

A [**studentized residual**]{style="color:blue"} is obtained when we scale a raw residual by an estimate for its standard error. When the error assumptions are satisfied, studentized residuals are a better judge of the potential size of an outlier.

A studentized residual is also called a [**jackknife** or **cross-validation residual**]{style="color:blue"} and is given by:

$$t_{(i)} = \frac{\widehat{\epsilon}_i}{\widehat{\sigma}_{(i)} \sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}  \sim t_{n-p-1} \qquad \text{where} \qquad \widehat{\sigma}_{(i)} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{RSS}_{(i)}}{n-p-1}}$$


```{r}
# studentized residual for Zambia
#sig <- sqrt(sum(residuals(loo_mod)^2) / (50 - 5 - 1))
sig <- summary(loo_mod)$sigma
residuals(lmod)[46]/(sig * sqrt( 1 - h[46]))
```



### Computing Studentized Residuals


```{r}
# obtain studentized residuals
stud <- rstudent(lmod)

# largest magnitude studentized residual
(max_stud <- max(abs(stud)))
```


### Plotting Studentized Residuals


```{r}
#library(car)
residualPlot(lmod, quadratic = FALSE, type = "rstudent") # against fitted
```


```{r}
plot(lmod, which = 3)
```


```{r}
#| warning: false
#library(car)
infIndexPlot(lmod, vars = "Studentized")
```

## Testing for Outliers


### Types of Errors and the Significance Level

There are two possible errors in a hypothesis test:

- A [**Type I Error**]{style="color:blue"} occurs if we incorrectly reject H~0~ (false positive).
- A [**Type II Error**]{style="color:blue"} occurs if we incorrectly fail to reject H~0~ (false negative).
- The [**significance level**]{style="color:blue"} of a hypothesis test is therefore the largest value of ${\color{blue} \alpha}$ we find acceptable for the probability for a Type I error.

We can test each observation separately:

- We test at the 5% significance level:
  - H~0~: Observation 1 is not an outlier.
  - H~a~: Observation 1 is an outlier.

- Then we perform another test at the 5% significance level.
  - H~0~: Observation 2 is not an outlier.
  - H~a~: Observation 2 is an outlier.


Or, we can test for multiple observations at the same time.

- H~0~: Neither observation 1 nor observation 2 are outliers.
- H~a~: Observation 1 or observation 2 is an outlier.

## Question 3 {#sec-q3}

What is the maximum value for the probability of making a Type I Error if the results of the two individual tests are significant.

### Solution to Question 3



<br>  
<br>  


### Bonferonni correction

Suppose we want a level $\alpha$ test for $n$ tests, i.e., we want P(no type I errors in n tests)$=1-\alpha$.  

$$\begin{align}
\mbox{P(no type I errors in all n tests)} &= P \left( \cap_{i=1}^n(\mbox{no type I error in test i}) \right)\\
&= 1 - P \left( \cup_{i=1}^n(\mbox{there IS type I error in test i}) \right)\\
& \geq 1 - \sum_{i=1}^n P(\mbox{there IS type I error in test i})\\
&= 1 - n\alpha
\end{align}$$

To get an overall level $\alpha$ test, we should use the level $\alpha/n$ in each of the individual tests.

- This approach is known as the [**Bonferonni correction**]{style="color:blue"}, and is used in many contexts to make proper simultaneous inference.
- The Bonferonni correction is a very conservative method.
  - It doesn’t reject H~0~ as often as it should.
  - It gets more conservative as $n$ gets larger.

A observation is considered an outlier if $|t_i| \geq t_{n-p-1}^{\frac{\alpha}{2n}}$.


### Computing Bonferonni Critical Values

```{r}
n_sav <- nrow(X)
p_sav <- ncol(X)
max_stud # maximum studentized residual from earlier
qt(1 - .05/(50*2), df = n_sav - p_sav - 1) # critical value
```

### Computing Bonferonni p-Values with outlierTest Function


```{r}
# perform outlier check using Bonferroni correction
outlierTest(lmod)
```


### Index Plots of Bonferroni p-values


```{r}
infIndexPlot(lmod, vars = "Bonf")
```


## Caution With Outliers:

- Two or more outliers next to each other can "hide" each other.
- If we fit a new model (on all data), we may get different or no outliers.
- If the error distribution is nonnormal, it is very reasonable to get large residuals.
- Individual outliers are less of a problem in larger data sets because they are not likely to have a large leverage.
  - It is still good to identify the outliers.
  - They probably won’t be an issue unless they occur in clusters.


# Influential Observations

Influential observations may be outliers, leverage points, or both outliers and leverage points. **leave-one-out residuals**, $\widehat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_{(i)} = y_i-\widehat{y}_{(i)}$, are one measure of influence.  We'll explore some others.

## Change in Regression Coefficients, DFBETA

- ${\color{blue}{\mbox{DFBETA}_i=\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} - \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(i)}}}$ is the difference in the estimated coefficients when leaving out the $i^{\text{th}}$ observation.
- It is a $p$-dimensional vector indicating how the estimated coefficients change when the $i^{\text{th}}$ observation is removed from the data.
- [**DFBETAS**]{style="color:blue"} is the DFBETA values divided by the leave-one-out estimate of the coefficient standard errors.

```{r}
lmod2 <- lm(sr ~ ., data = savings, subset = (countries != "Libya"))
compareCoefs(lmod, lmod2)  # requires car package
```

### Ploting DFBETA and DFBETAs 


An index plot of the DFBETA statistics can be useful for assessing the direct impact of an observation on the estimated coefficients.

```{r}
#library(car) # required package loaded earlier
#dfbetaPlots(lmod, id.n = 3, lab = countries) # Not standardized
dfbetasPlots(lmod, id.n = 3, lab = countries) # Standardized
```


## Cook's Distance

The [**Cook’s distance**]{style="color:blue"} is a popular inferential tool because it reduces influence information to a single value for each observation.

The Cook’s distance for the $i^{\text{th}}$ observation is

$$D_i=\frac{(\widehat{\mathbf{y}} - \widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{(i)})^T(\widehat{\mathbf{y}} - \widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{(i)})}{p \widehat{\sigma}^2} = \frac{1}{p} r_i^2 \frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}}$$

where $r_i$ the **standardized residual** or observation $i$ (has mean 0 and variance 1):

$$r_i = \frac{y_i - \widehat{y}_i}{\widehat{\sigma}(1-h_i)}.$$

Notice that the statistic considers both:

- The standardized residual (measurement of outlier).
- The leverage (as measured by the hat value $h_{ii}$).
- The combination of the two leads to a potentially influential value.

### Interpreting Cook's Distance

- Larger values of Cook’s Distance indicate more influence on the regression results.
- Recommended criteria for identifying influential observations with Cook’s Distance are: 
  - $D \geq  0.5$ may be influential.
  - $D \geq 1$ likely to be influential.
  - If it stands out (in index plot or half-normal plot), it very likely influential regardless of the value.
  - $D \geq \dfrac{4}{n-p}$ or $D \geq 2 \sqrt{p/n}$ are other criteria that takes into account the size of the sample and number of regressors.

For the savings model, we have $n=50$, $p=5$. We can use $D \geq 0.089$ or $D \geq 0.632$ as other criteria.


### Computing and Plotting Cook's Distance

- Cook’s distance values can be obtained using the `cooks.distance() ` function.
- A half-normal plot of the Cook’s distances can be used to identify influential observation in the same way we used it for leverage values.


```{r}
cook <- cooks.distance(lmod)
halfnorm(cook, n = 3, labs = countries, ylab = "Cook's distances")
```


- An index plot of the Cook’s distances can be used to identify influential observations.

```{r}
#| warning: false
infIndexPlot(lmod, var = "Cook", id = list(n = 3))
```


## Influence Plots

An [**influence plot**]{style="color:blue"} plots the studentized residuals versus the leverage values.

- The `influencePlot()` function from `car` can be used to create this.
- Look for observations that have unusually large residuals, leverage values, and especially both.

# What Should We Do About Unusual Observations?


```{r}
compareCoefs(lmod, lmod2)
```


```{r}
plot(dfbeta(lmod)[,5], ylab = "Change in ddpi coef")
abline(h=0)
text(dfbeta(lmod)[,5], labels=rownames(savings), cex=0.6, font=0.5)
```


## Should We Correct or Delete the Observation(s)?

- **If they’re data entry errors**, either correct the problem or remove them if they can't be corrected. 
  - They’re wrong, so they don’t tell us anything useful!
- **If they are NOT part of the population of interest**, remove them.
  - For example, you are studying dogs, but this observation is a cat.
- **Removing them just because they break the model is a really bad idea!**
  - If you do, make sure to indicate that you removed them from the data set and explain why.
  - Be warned, it is generally going to be a bad idea to remove.
- The best solution is to try to **understand influential observations**.

## Should We Keep Them and Fit a Different Model?

- An outlier/influential point for one model may not be for another.
- Examine the physical context, why did it happen?
  - An outlier/influential point may be interesting in itself. 
  - For example, an outlier in a statistical analysis of credit card transactions may indicate fraud.
- Applying a square root or (natural) log transformation to a strategically selected regressor(s) might help.
  - This may lead to another (better) model.
- Use **robust regression**, which is not as affected by outliers/influential observations.


## Summary

- Never automatically remove outliers/influential points!
- They may provide important information that may otherwise be missed.
- Fit the model with and without the influential observation(s).
- Do your results substantively change?

# Appendix: Properties of Leverage Values {#sec-append}

## Proof that $0 \leq h_{ii} \leq 1$

Since the hat matrix $H$ is idempotent ($H^2 = H$) and symmetric, we have:

$$h_{ii} = h_{ii}^2 + \sum_{i \ne j} h_{ij}^2.$$

Thus, $h_{ii} \geq h_{ii}^2$, which implies $0 \leq h_{ii} < 1$. 


## Proof that $\sum h_{ii} = p$

We have 

$$\begin{align}
\sum h_{ii} &= \text{Tr}(H) \tag{def. of trace}\\
& = \text{Tr}(X(X^T X)^{-1} X^T) \tag{def. of hat matrix}\\
&= \text{Tr}(X^T X (X^T X)^{-1} ) \tag{cyclic property of trace}\\
&= \text{Tr}(\mathbf{I}_p) \tag{product of inverses}\\
&= p.
\end{align}$$

# Methods for Identifying Unusual Observations

## Leverage points:

- Half-normal plot of leverage values
- Index plot of leverage values

## Outliers

- Bonferonni outlier test
- Index plot of studentized residuals

## Influential observations:

- Half-normal plot of Cook’s distances
- Index plot of Cook’s distances
- Index plot of DFBETA or DFBETAS.
- Influence plot

# Useful R functions for Identifying Unusual Observations

## Leverage points

- `hatvalues` extracts the leverage values from a fitted model.
- `faraway::halfnorm` constructs a half-normal plot
- `infIndexPlot(lmod, vars = "hat")` creates an index plot of the leverage values.

## Outliers

- `car::outlierTest` performs a Bonferonni outlier test
- `infIndexPlot(lmod, vars = "Studentized")` creates an index plot of the studentized residuals.

## Influential observations

- `cooks.distance` extracts the Cook’s distances from a fitted model.
- `faraway::halfnorm` constructs a half-normal plot
- `infIndexPlot(lmod, vars = "Cook")` constructs an index plot of the Cook’s distances.
- `plot(lmod, which = 4)` constructs an index plot of the Cook’s statistics.
- `car::dfbetaPlots` and `car::dfbetasPlots` construct index plots of DFBETA and DFBETAS, respectively.
- `car::influencePlot` constructs an influence plot of the studentized residuals versus the leverage values.
- `plot(lmod, which = 4)` constructs an influence plot of the standardized residuals versus the leverage values.
- `influence(lmod)` computes a number of leave-one-out-related measures of observational influence.
